topics.title: Nicaragua v. Germany at the ICJ: Jurisdiction, Third-State Responsibility, and Complicity in Arms Transfers
topics.framing: Nicaragua brought a case against Germany at the ICJ alleging that German arms transfers to Israel facilitate genocide in Gaza. Germany filed preliminary objections to jurisdiction and admissibility, and oral hearings on those preliminary questions were held 7-10 September 2026. A separate strand of commentary debates the temporal scope of Germany's ICJ declaration and the standards for third-state complicity under Article 16 of the ILC Articles on State Responsibility.
topics.mainstream_view: The proceedings are a normal exercise of ICJ jurisdiction and admissibility doctrine: Germany's preliminary objections raise technical questions of consent, temporal limitation (ratione temporis), and the Monetary Gold principle, which the Court must resolve before reaching the merits. Third-state responsibility for arms transfers is governed by established secondary rules, including Article 16, and the fault threshold for complicity is higher than for prevention, so the legal risk to supplying states is real but bounded and litigated through ordinary judicial channels.
topics.global_south_view: The case exposes how structural inequality operates in international adjudication: powerful states can delay and deflect merits review through procedural objections, while the substantive question of complicity in grave breaches of peremptory norms is deferred. From this perspective, the ICJ's handling of jurisdiction and temporality becomes a site where the enforcement gap for third-state responsibility is reproduced, and the provisional measures order is read as a meaningful but limited constraint on continued arms transfers.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides accept the doctrinal framework of jurisdiction and Article 16 complicity, but they diverge sharply on whether procedural deferral reflects neutral adjudication or structural shielding of powerful states.

topics.title: Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems and the CCW GGE: Characterisation, Regulation, and the Future of LAWS Governance
topics.framing: The CCW Group of Governmental Experts on LAWS is operating under a three-year mandate running through 2026, with its final report expected to feed into the Seventh Review Conference in Geneva on 16-20 November 2026. Delegations remain sharply divided on the rolling text, and the Review Conference will decide whether to move toward a legally binding instrument, extend the discussion-only mandate, or let the process lapse. No binding international agreement on LAWS has yet been adopted.
topics.mainstream_view: The GGE process is the appropriate forum for incremental, consensus-based progress, and the Chair's rolling text and set of elements represent meaningful steps toward a normative and operational framework. Existing IHL rules already apply to LAWS, and the priority is to build common understandings, retain human responsibility in judgment and oversight, and avoid premature binding commitments that major military powers would reject.
topics.global_south_view: The consensus-based CCW process structurally advantages militarily advanced states, allowing a handful of major powers to block a binding instrument while autonomous weapons move toward routine deployment. From this perspective, the failure to reach a treaty by the 2026 deadline reflects not technical complexity but a governance design that subordinates humanitarian protection to the strategic interests of the most powerful states.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides agree that existing IHL applies and that the 2026 Review Conference is pivotal, but they diverge on whether the GGE's consensus model is a virtue or a structural obstacle to meaningful regulation.

topics.title: AI and International Law: Sovereignty, Due Diligence, and State Responsibility in the Digital Age
topics.framing: Scholarship and institutional reports are exploring how AI interacts with state sovereignty, due diligence, and state responsibility, including whether designating AI tools and infrastructure as critical infrastructure triggers obligations of risk mitigation and notification. The ILC has been advancing work on due diligence as a concept at the interface of primary rules and secondary rules of state responsibility, and the OHCHR has issued a report on human rights due diligence for AI. Debate continues over whether a positive obligation to regulate AI can be grounded in existing international law.
topics.mainstream_view: Existing international law, including the ILC Articles on State Responsibility and human rights due diligence standards, already provides a workable framework for AI governance. States have obligations to respect, protect, and fulfil human rights, and due diligence requires systemic and continuing risk assessment; the precautionary principle can support regulatory action, and international cooperation, open standards, and shared research are necessary because no state can build every AI component alone.
topics.global_south_view: Digital sovereignty is both an internal normative act and a claim to power in a context where multinational corporations wield substantial governance authority through internal policies and codes of conduct. From this perspective, due diligence frameworks developed without attention to structural asymmetries risk legitimizing the dominance of a few technologically advanced states and firms, and the legal question is whether states can preserve democratic control and regulatory autonomy while participating in global technological systems shaped by others.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides accept that due diligence and state responsibility frameworks apply to AI, but they differ on whether those frameworks are adequate to address the power asymmetries that shape AI governance.

topics.title: Structural Inequality and Selective Enforcement in International Humanitarian Law: CCF and the Global South
topics.framing: Commentary on Iran's strikes on Kurdish parties examines the unenforceability of the customary rule on civilian-combatant distinction (CCF) and argues that even a clear finding of a CCF violation would depend on the belligerent state's consent to enforcement. Broader scholarship documents structural biases and barriers facing the Global South in international law, including in international criminal law's complementarity assessments, and debates whether the Global South can salvage the system through collective action.
topics.mainstream_view: IHL violations are addressed through established mechanisms, including fact-finding missions, the ICRC, and where applicable international criminal proceedings, and the CCF rule remains a foundational principle of distinction. Enforcement gaps are acknowledged but are treated as matters of state consent and institutional capacity rather than as evidence of systemic bias, and reforms are pursued incrementally through existing bodies.
topics.global_south_view: The unenforceability of CCF is a symptom of structural inequality in IHL: enforcement depends on the belligerent state's consent, and the system's design allows powerful states to selectively ignore or violate international law while marginalized states face scrutiny. From this perspective, international criminal law's complementarity assessments reproduce old tropes about Global South states' inability to govern themselves, and tangible reforms are needed to remove structural barriers and restore trust in the system.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides recognize enforcement gaps in IHL, but they diverge on whether those gaps are technical problems or evidence of structural bias that requires systemic reform.

topics.title: Sovereignty over Plant Genetic Resources and Food Security: The ITPGRFA Package Deal and TWAIL Critiques
topics.framing: The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (2001) established a multilateral system for open access to plant genetic resources, a principle of Farmers' Rights recognizing farmers as holders of traditional knowledge and stewards of agricultural biodiversity, and conservation obligations covering on-farm conservation and seed banks. TWAIL scholarship examines the 'package deal' and the treaty's future through the lens of negotiated sovereignty, while other work debates what kind of goods plant genetic resources are and whether a new global commons framework is needed.
topics.mainstream_view: The Plant Treaty is a successful example of multilateral cooperation that balances access to genetic resources with benefit-sharing and food security, and its multilateral system provides predictable open access for breeders and researchers. Farmers' Rights and conservation obligations are integrated into the treaty framework, and the priority is to strengthen implementation and adapt the treaty to evolving needs.
topics.global_south_view: The treaty's 'package deal' reflects negotiated sovereignty in which developing countries traded access to genetic resources for recognition of Farmers' Rights and benefit-sharing, but the balance has been uneven in practice. From this perspective, the framing of plant genetic resources as a global commons can obscure the sovereignty claims of source countries and the food sovereignty concerns of farming communities, and the treaty's future depends on correcting asymmetries in how benefits and obligations are distributed.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides value the treaty's multilateral system and Farmers' Rights, but they differ on whether the package deal has delivered equitable outcomes or reproduced asymmetries between source countries and users of genetic resources.

topics.title: Climate Change, the Future of the State, and International Economic Law: Global South Perspectives
topics.framing: Scholarship and lectures are examining how international law and international economic law shape responses to climate change, including questions of reparations, the background rules of international law, and the threatened sovereignty of island states facing rising sea levels. Anne Orford's LRIL lecture addresses climate change and the future of the state, and other work explores how international economic law might adapt to allow Global South states to exit or modify economic relationships that increase their climate vulnerability. Climate litigation in the Global South faces distinctive constraints.
topics.mainstream_view: Climate change is addressed through the existing international legal architecture, including the UNFCCC framework, human rights law, and dispute settlement, and international economic law can adapt through existing flexibilities and negotiated reforms. State sovereignty provides both the basis for and a constraint on climate action, and the priority is to strengthen cooperation, reparations frameworks, and the background rules that structure state responsibility.
topics.global_south_view: Global South states are disproportionately impacted by climate change yet face structural constraints in international economic law that lock them into relationships increasing their vulnerability, and many have historically prioritized immediate development, poverty reduction, and energy security over climate action. From this perspective, the future of the state and the background rules of international law must be rethought to allow meaningful exit or modification of those relationships, and climate litigation in the Global South confronts distinctive constraints that Northern-centric frameworks overlook.
topics.convergence_note: Both sides recognize the need for climate action and the relevance of international economic law, but they diverge on whether existing frameworks are adequate or whether structural reform is needed to address Global South vulnerability.
